title: Deterministic relative counting for DNF
formal:
Is there a deterministic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for the number of satisfying assignments of an arbitrary explicitly given DNF formula? In the precise reciprocal-integer accuracy convention used here, do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) and positive integers \(C,a\) such that for every DNF formula \(\varphi\) of encoding length \(N\) over its declared \(n\) variables, and every integer \(q\ge2\), the algorithm outputs a nonnegative rational number \(\widehat Z\) with
\[|\widehat Z-Z(\varphi)|\le Z(\varphi)/q,\qquad Z(\varphi)=|\{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\varphi(x)=1\}|,\]
and halts within \(C(N+q+1)^a\) steps? The guarantee must hold on every input without randomness, advice or an oracle. There is no bound on term width or on the number of occurrences of a variable other than the explicit input length.
why: DNF counting is a canonical approximate-counting problem for which randomization gives an efficient relative approximation even when direct random assignment sampling rarely finds a solution. A deterministic scheme would remove randomness from this basic union-counting task across all formula widths and occurrence patterns. It would strengthen the explicit derandomization tools available for both complexity theory and probabilistic data processing.
status_note: The source algorithm and both numbered restatements were read directly on 2026-09-14. The bounded later search through 2026 found restricted and randomized approximate-counting results but no deterministic fully polynomial relative-counting scheme for arbitrary DNF. Trevisan’s constant-width result and the full Servedio–Tan read-k manuscript were checked for the relevant distinction. No exhaustive current-openness certification is claimed.

sentences: A DNF formula describes a union of sets of Boolean assignments, one set for each conjunction.
The question asks for deterministic relative approximation of the number of assignments in that union.
One uniform algorithm must run in time polynomial in the explicit formula size and reciprocal error.
The estimate must count assignments once despite overlapping terms and must be exactly zero for an unsatisfiable formula.
Randomized schemes and deterministic algorithms for restricted formulas leave the general fully polynomial target unresolved in the checked sources.

definitions:
A literal is a declared variable \(x_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), or its negation. A term is a finite conjunction of literals; a DNF formula is a finite disjunction of terms. All literal occurrences and all terms are listed explicitly. Empty conjunctions evaluate to true and the empty disjunction evaluates to false. Repeated literals or terms are allowed, and a term containing both signs of one variable is false. A variable assignment specifies every declared variable, including unused ones; every satisfying assignment is counted once regardless of how many terms it satisfies.

Use an explicit encoding consisting of \(1^n\), a self-delimiting binary term count, and for each term its self-delimiting literal count followed by variable indices in binary and one sign bit per literal. Thus the declared variable set is part of the input, \(n\le N\), and arbitrary circuits or compressed representations of an exponentially larger DNF are excluded. Valid formulas with \(n=0\) are included and are evaluated on the unique empty assignment. Malformed encodings may be rejected in polynomial time and are not counted as instances of the formula problem.

The accuracy parameter \(q\) is given in binary. Computation uses a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine; one transition costs one step, and writing the output is counted. Represent \(\widehat Z\) by a binary nonnegative numerator and positive denominator. They need not be in lowest terms. The constants in the running-time bound are independent of the formula, its width, its variable occurrence counts and \(q\). All preprocessing is included.

The target is relative error \(1/q\). This is the usual fully polynomial accuracy convention: an arbitrary requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) can be met by taking \(q=\max\{2,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\), with the time to read that request also counted. The runtime is polynomial in the reciprocal accuracy, not merely its bit length. If \(Z=0\), the output must equal zero exactly. If \(Z>0\), it must lie between \((1-1/q)Z\) and \((1+1/q)Z\). Additive error \(2^n/q\) is a different and potentially much weaker guarantee when satisfying assignments are rare. The algorithm is allowed to output a rational estimate; exact integer counting is not required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of this deterministic approximation scheme. A positive answer must specify the algorithm and prove its relative-error and fully polynomial-time guarantees for all formulas and all \(q\ge2\), including zero counts. A negative answer must rule out every such uniform deterministic scheme. Randomized high-probability estimates, an additive-error approximation alone, quasipolynomial runtime, or polynomial algorithms restricted to bounded-width or bounded-occurrence formulas do not settle the full target.

context_blocks.text: The source’s randomized Algorithm 2.35 gives a relative approximation in time polynomial in formula size and reciprocal accuracy. Open Problems 2.36 and 7.32 ask for deterministic polynomial time, with the latter discussion supplying a quasipolynomial-time derandomization baseline.

Overlaps between terms are essential: adding the numbers of assignments satisfying the individual terms can count the same assignment many times. The problem counts the size of their union, with all declared variables included.

Trevisan gives deterministic multiplicative approximation in time linear in formula length and polynomial in reciprocal accuracy when term width is a fixed constant. Its dependence on that width does not provide a uniform polynomial bound for arbitrary DNF inputs.

Servedio and Tan study formulas in which each variable occurs at most k times, a restriction different from term width. Their relative-error algorithms have explicit dependence on k and accuracy; their results do not furnish the all-occurrence fully polynomial bound required here.

notes: Recovered the relative-error fully polynomial target from Algorithm 2.35 and the paired Open Problems 2.36 and 7.32.
Specified explicit DNF encoding, declared and unused variables, term overlap, degenerate formulas, rational outputs and exact behavior at zero count.
Made reciprocal accuracy and uniform deterministic bit-model runtime precise, without confusing polynomial reciprocal-error dependence with polynomial precision-bit dependence.
Separated randomized schemes, additive approximation, constant term width and bounded variable occurrence results from arbitrary DNF counting.
